The Promise

The origin of terms and conditions

Stage 1

Then, promises had to reach more people.

As businesses grew, they began displaying notices that stated their conditions and limits. These made it possible to communicate the same terms to many customers at once, but only if customers had a reasonable chance to see them.

Stage 2

But when did those terms actually count?

Courts developed rules around how contractual terms were communicated and accepted. Whether a customer had been given adequate notice mattered: a condition could not simply become part of an agreement because a business had written it down.

Stage 3

Trust began with people.

Before businesses served customers at scale, agreements were often shaped through direct dealings. Buyers and sellers could ask questions, negotiate conditions and rely on each other’s reputation. Trust was built through the relationship itself.

Stage 4

Introducing standard terms

Industrialisation made individual negotiation impractical. Standard terms brought efficiency and consistency, filled gaps in agreements and helped businesses allocate risk. The same conditions could now govern countless transactions, even between strangers.

Article on Origin of Standard terms

The framework made large-scale transactions more predictable. But it left a tension: having access to terms does not mean someone has read, understood or had the power to negotiate them.

A paper that questions the effectiveness of standard form contracts

As agreements moved onto digital platforms, what would happen to the meaning of consent when accepting could take just one tap?

The Transformation

How digital platforms changed the way terms are presented and accepted.

Stage 1

Terms began governing entire digital environments.

As platforms grew, their terms expanded beyond the company–user relationship to cover data privacy, content moderation, account access, payment rules and recovery mechanisms. Many of these rules mattered most when something went wrong.

Stage 2

The terms were available. But were they understood?

Digital platforms made legal terms easy to present and easy to accept. Yet the experience of engaging with them changed:

  • Visibility: Important conditions could sit behind small links, several screens or general policies.
  • Readability: Policies grew lengthy and complex, while users had limited time and attention.
Paper on how long digital privacy policies tend to be
Stage 3

The agreement moved onto the screen.

Online services made it possible to form agreements through buttons, checkboxes and account creation. Accepting terms became part of using a product, making contracts faster and easier to establish at scale.

Stage 4

Frictionless acceptance

Clickwrap, browsewrap and in-app consent mechanisms changed how users encountered terms. Legal acceptance could now happen through a checkbox, a link or continued use, often designed to keep the main task moving with minimal interruption.

Experimental survey on digital acceptance interaction behaviors

Digital platforms need terms to define their rules, allocate responsibilities and protect their services. But when agreement is embedded in everyday interactions, the act of accepting can become disconnected from understanding what has been accepted.

As money moved into digital environments, what new responsibilities did the terms need to account for?

The Stakes

The responsibilities of financial digital platforms.

Stage 1

Who is responsible when a transaction goes wrong?

A digital payment depends on more than the app on a user's screen. Banks, payment-system operators, technology providers and merchants all play different roles. The rules governing these services must define how systems operate, how responsibilities are distributed, and how failures and disputes are addressed.

Stage 2

When money moved online

As financial services moved into digital environments, payments could be initiated through apps and processed across interconnected systems. In India, the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 established a legal framework for the regulation and supervision of payment systems by the RBI.

Stage 3

The rules protecting users are often the rules they struggle to find.

Terms and legal frameworks help establish safeguards, allocate responsibility and explain what happens when something goes wrong. Yet this information can be buried in lengthy policies, divided across multiple institutions or difficult to understand at the moment a user needs it most.

The Contradiction

How terms and conditions can become barriers to understanding and trust.

Terms and conditions are meant to make expectations, responsibilities and protections clear. But in digital financial products, trust is shaped by more than the information provided. It is also shaped by what users are asked to share, how the rules are framed, and when and where the information appears.

When these choices make important information difficult to find, understand or act upon, the very mechanisms designed to establish trust can begin to undermine it.

So, what happens to trust when we look beyond what information is provided, and examine how it is handled throughout the user journey?

The Position

What we believe trust should look like in digital financial products.

In a system where users have little choice but to trust digital platforms, we believe it must be earned and not assumed.

So, what shapes trust in digital financial products, and where does it begin to break down?

Explore what our findings reveal, how Edelman’s research helps us understand these breakdowns, and the principles we believe should guide more trustworthy design.

TRUST & INTENT

What we learned

01

Trust is earned on the screen and spent in the contract.

~ challenge card 01 & 05

What Edelman found

02

“People increasingly trust only those closest to them, and a trusted voice can make them trust something they otherwise wouldn’t.”

So when PhonePe speaks like a friend but acts like a stranger in its terms, it feels like betrayal.

So what we believe

03
Sharing is only trust if users know who they’re sharing with. A platform that lends its trust should stand behind it.

ACCESS & VISIBILITY

What we learned

01

Information can be available without being accessible.

~ challenge card 04 & 06

What Edelman found

02

“When people feel left out or excluded, they start to feel the system is rigged against them, and the trust gap between richer and poorer people keeps growing.”

So hidden rules hurt most those who can least afford a surprise, and confirm that the system isn’t built for them.

So what we believe

03
Information that only some users can perceive hasn’t truly been displayed. A notice the user never sees is not notice.

CONSENT & CONTROL

What we learned

01

Trust is tested when users wants to leave or something goes wrong.

~ challenge card 02 & 03

What Edelman found

02

“People come to trust others when they’ve been helped or supported by them, and lose trust when the system feels set against them.”

So the moments PhonePe is absent, leaving and failing, are exactly the moments it could have earned trust.

So what we believe

03
Consent that can’t be withdrawn as easily as it was given isn’t real consent. Trust is proven when something goes wrong, not when everything works.

POV

In India, where digital payments are part of everyday life, people often keep using platforms out of necessity, not trust. These platforms are designed for the best-case scenario, but trust is revealed in how they treat people when things don’t go as expected.

Terms and Conditions, once meant to define relationships, have increasingly become tools to protect platforms rather than help users understand them. The trust they were meant to establish is now being challenged.

We believe trust must be rebuilt by closing the gap between what platforms promise on paper and what users actually experience on screen. Because trust isn’t established by terms alone, but with various other factors that accompany it.

In the next section, we explore how this trust can be re-established.
